job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in construction management at Ashby College, and I live with my parents in Elmhurst and take the train in four days a week. In the evenings I help my dad, who is a builder with a team of six, with his estimates and his paperwork. On Sundays we go to church and then to my grandmother's for lunch. I'm engaged to Tomas, and we're planning a wedding next summer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He's a clerk at a bank branch in Elmhurst, handling loans and accounts. My bachelor's in civil engineering was a pass, and I never did an internship, but I spent most summers on my dad's sites, so I know what a site looks like. I don't use AI tools, and I'm happy to leave them alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought, and good. We should get on with building and working, and not be distracted by headlines. I'd tell my friends at church that prices and rents matter more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan holds. I finish the master's, join a building contractor as a site engineer or assistant project manager, and learn the trade properly. Tomas keeps his bank job, my parents keep their health, and we get married. I have no debt and over six months saved, so it feels safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my dissertation on site safety planning and apply to about eight builders around Elmhurst, including two big ones in the city. I'd keep helping Dad with estimates on Saturdays and learn the contract side. Tomas and I would look at a small house to rent after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little proud. It's the life I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your plans for the wedding change in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't. We'd still marry in June at St Anne's, with sixty guests, and my mother's cooking. Paying for it from savings feels fine, and my parents are helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your dad's firm like at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's busy but not rich. Dad has work booked three months ahead, and two of his men are near retirement. Dad says there are not enough young people who want to learn a trade, which is partly why he's glad I'm in it.

say: That's what I thought, and good: **get on with building** and ignore headlines.
I'd tell friends at church that **prices and rents** matter more than robots.
think: My plan holds: finish the master's and join a builder as a **site engineer**.
I have no debt and over **six months saved**, so it feels safe.
do: Finish my dissertation on **site safety** and apply to about eight builders.
Keep helping Dad with **estimates** and look for a small rented house.
feel: Calm and a little **proud**: it's the life I wanted.
S0.quote: Dad says there are not enough young people who want to learn a trade, which is partly why he's glad I'm in it.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **family, faith** and a trade, which is her traditional view of a good life.
Mentions her father's shortage of young tradespeople as a **source of pride**.

steps.text: Finish the dissertation on site safety planning
Apply to eight builders near Elmhurst
Keep doing estimates with Dad on Saturdays
Look at small houses to rent after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say work still matters, and young people should learn something with their hands and their head. I'd say AI can't tile a bathroom, and I'd say it at church and at the college. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy. The planning, estimating and paperwork part of construction is what the tools do first, and that's my master's. Tomas's bank clerk work is the first to shrink, and I'd worry about our income together more than mine. My degree is only a pass, so I'd lean on site experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the site side of my degree, apply for site engineer roles rather than office ones, and keep helping Dad. I'd ask Tomas whether his bank might retrain him, and I'd put a bit more into savings. I wouldn't touch AI tools unless my employer made me, and then I'd learn one thing at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can handle my own job, but our household's second income worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tomas's job be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Tomas's bank branch already closes on Wednesday afternoons, and the manager talks about the loan software doing the checking. Tomas says nobody has been let go yet, but they haven't hired in a year. He's trying to take a course in financial advice, which I'd encourage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about AI in estimating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad it can do an estimate in ten minutes, but it can't know that Mr Brennan's wall is damp. He'd laugh and agree. He'd still check the software's number against his own, which is the right way.

say: Work still matters, and young people should learn with their **hands and head**.
I'd say AI can't **tile a bathroom**.
think: Planning, estimating and paperwork go first, and that's **my master's**.
Tomas's bank clerk work shrinks first, which worries me about our **joint income**.
do: Apply for **site engineer** roles rather than office ones.
Ask Tomas about **bank retraining** and put more into savings.
feel: Uneasy: I can handle my job, but our **second income** worries me.
S1.quote: My fiancé Tomas's bank branch already closes on Wednesday afternoons, and the manager talks about the loan software doing the checking.
fieldNote: Her worry is about the **household**: her fiancé's clerk job is more exposed than her site work.
Keeps her resistance to AI but accepts she'd learn **one thing** at a time if forced.

steps.text: Apply for site engineer roles rather than office jobs
Encourage Tomas to take a financial advice course
Raise the monthly savings by a hundred pounds
Learn one estimating tool only if an employer requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, that people should be protected before companies save money. I'd say it at church and at the town meeting, and I'd write to our councillor and our member of parliament. Our community has always looked after its own, and that has to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be terrified. If AI does any thinking job by 2028, a bank clerk's job could be gone within a year or two. Robots come about 2031, which would hit even my father's work in time. I'd be left with a wedding, a mortgage dream and one income that might vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding plan to something smaller and keep every penny of savings. I'd ask my parents if Tomas and I could live with them for a year after we marry. I'd take any site job I could get, even a poor one, and help Tomas find work with hands, maybe as a plumber's mate with Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wake at four in the morning and do sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit him down in my mother's kitchen and say, we'll manage, but we need to decide what to do before the bank decides for you. He'd go quiet. He'd say he's the one who's supposed to be steady, and I'd say we both are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get married next summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry him, yes, but I'd make it a quieter day. Sixty guests becomes thirty, and the money goes to a cushion. If the future is that uncertain, then I want the vows more, not less.

say: This is wrong: people should be **protected** before companies save money.
I'd write to our councillor and our **member of parliament**.
think: A bank clerk's job could be gone within **a year or two**, leaving one income.
Robots around 2031 would hit even **my father's** work in time.
do: Shrink the wedding and keep every penny of **savings**.
Ask my parents if we can live with them for **a year**.
feel: Alarmed: I wake at four and do **sums** in my head.
S2.quote: If the future is that uncertain, then I want the vows more, not less.
fieldNote: Her **traditional** values show in the wedding choice: marry anyway, but smaller.
The fear is about **Tomas's job** and the shared income, not about herself.

steps.text: Cut the wedding from sixty guests to thirty
Keep all the savings as a cushion
Ask my parents if we can live with them for a year
Write to our councillor and member of parliament about protection for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are honest and sensible. I'd tell young people to learn a trade as a backup. At church I'd ask the minister to run a skills evening for the congregation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think we'd have a few years of normal life. Tomas's bank job might last two or three years, and then the pressure arrives. I'd be nervous but not frightened, because I'd have built up savings and a site career before it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned and start site work. Tomas would do a course in financial advice or building inspection, something people still need. I'd save a third of my pay, buy a small house rather than rent, and keep helping Dad. I'd learn the software only when I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Five years is like knowing a storm is coming and having time to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you do with Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the order. With two years I'd cut the wedding and move in with my parents. With five I'd marry, work, save and get Tomas into a second skill early. We'd have a few good years, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want from your church or town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my church for a mentoring scheme, where older tradespeople teach younger ones for free. I'd want the town to run training for adults at night, like it used to. People here look after one another, and I'd want that to do some work.

say: Five years is enough to prepare if people are **honest and sensible**.
I'd ask our minister to run a **skills evening**.
think: Tomas's bank job might last **two or three years**, and then pressure arrives.
I'd be nervous, not frightened, with **savings** and a site career built first.
do: Marry next summer and save a third of my pay for a **small house**.
Help Tomas train in **building inspection** or financial advice.
feel: Anxious but steady: a **storm** coming and time to fix the roof.
S3.quote: Five years is like knowing a storm is coming and having time to fix the roof.
fieldNote: Time lets her keep the **wedding** and the life she planned, with a second skill added for Tomas.
Looks to the **church and town** for mentoring, a traditional answer to a modern problem.

steps.text: Marry next summer as planned and start site work
Help Tomas train in building inspection
Save a third of my pay towards a small house
Ask our church to start a mentoring scheme for trades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it well. I'd tell young people to build character and skills, and not to rely on any one job. I'd say it at church, and I'd back leaders who talk about work and family together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little uneasy, but not much. I'd be thirty-four by 2036 with years of site experience, maybe a project manager, and probably children. Robots around 2039 would arrive in my forties, and I'd be one of the people who knows how a site really works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work on sites for a few years, and become a project manager. Tomas would train and get a steady job. We'd buy a house and start our family around 2030. I'd use new software only when my firm has proved it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Ten years is long enough that I stop bracing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the job and the wedding done first, then the house, then the children. If the world gets strange later, I'd rather meet it with a house, a husband and a family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about most for your children, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry they'd grow up in a world where nobody needs to learn a trade, and then nobody knows what a good day's work feels like. I'd teach my children to lay a brick, to bake bread and to say thank you. Those aren't going out of date.

say: Ten years is a **blessing**, so we should use it well.
I'd back leaders who talk about **work and family** together.
think: By 2036 I'd have **years of site experience**, maybe as a project manager.
Robots around 2039 arrive in my forties, and I'd know how a **site really works**.
do: Work on building sites for several years and become a **project manager**.
Buy a house with Tomas and start our **family** around 2030.
feel: Uneasy, but mostly fine: ten years is long enough that I **stop bracing**.
S4.quote: I'd teach my children to lay a brick, to bake bread and to say thank you. Those aren't going out of date.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her place **marriage, house and children** in order, and she keeps tools at arm's length.
Her fear for the next generation is about **meaning of work**, not only income.

steps.text: Work on sites for a few years and become a project manager
Buy a house and start a family around 2030
Back leaders who link work and family at the ballot box
Use new software only after the firm has proved it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because Tomas's job and our wedding are tied up in it, and my savings can't cover a lost income for long. What would help is honest warning from banks and employers, and training for people already working, paid for by the firms that save the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd only say that I'm not against machines. I just think a person should still be able to get an honest day's work and be proud of it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against machines. I just think a person should still be able to get an honest day's work and be proud of it.
portrait: Chloe is a **24-year-old** construction management master's student who lives with her parents and is engaged to Tomas.
Her father is a builder, her faith and family come first, and she **never uses AI tools**.
She is traditional and resistant: she wants **work, apprenticeships** and community support, not handouts.
Her mood runs from calm to **alarmed** in the two-year world, where Tomas's bank job is the first at risk.
She plans with a small wedding, a **cushion** and a second skill for Tomas.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because Tomas's job and the wedding are tied together and her savings couldn't replace a lost income for long.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **warning** from banks and employers, and training paid for by the firms that save the money.
